bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Intensifying competition and consequent pricing pressure — The AR flags a highly competitive diagnostics industry where national diagnostic chains, hospital-based laboratories, regional standalone players and digital-first healthcare platforms are expanding aggressively, which may cause pricing pressure, loss of market share and margin contraction in the Company's key operating regions. Management separately lists pricing risk from competition, customer expectations and potential regulatory intervention, and notes that unorganised, low-cost participants create pricing pressure and can dilute brand perception on quality and pricing standards.
- Execution risk in the network expansion strategy — Growth depends on adding new centres and laboratories, which exposes the Company to delays in operationalisation, lower-than-expected utilisation, longer gestation periods and variability in the performance of new centres - all of which can weigh on short-term profitability. This is the direct counterweight to the stated plan of expanding to 100 centres by FY28 and entering Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities beyond Eastern India.
- Geographic concentration in Eastern and North-Eastern India — The Company describes itself as one of the largest full-service integrated diagnostic chains in Eastern India, headquartered in Kolkata, with its operating network across West Bengal, Bihar, Assam and Meghalaya. Earnings are therefore tied to demand, competition and regulation in a single contiguous region, and the diversification remedy the AR points to - Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities beyond Eastern India - is still a plan rather than an established base.
- Dependence on scarce skilled medical professionals and attrition — The business is heavily dependent on experienced radiologists, pathologists, technicians and healthcare professionals; shortage of qualified personnel, rising attrition or an inability to attract and retain talent may impair service quality and operational efficiency. Management also flags that limited availability of adequately trained technicians and specialised personnel in new geographies may itself slow the pace of expansion, forcing redeployment of experienced staff from existing centres.
- Regulatory, pricing-control and data-protection compliance burden — The Company operates in a highly regulated environment subject to healthcare and diagnostic laws, regulations and quality standards. Changes in government regulations, pricing controls, data protection requirements or healthcare policies may raise compliance costs and reduce operational flexibility; mitigation rests on internal compliance mechanisms, compliance audits and monitoring of regulatory developments.
- Technological obsolescence in radiology, pathology and molecular diagnostics — Rapid advances in diagnostic technology require continuous investment in equipment upgrades and technology integration; failure to adopt evolving technologies may erode service quality and competitiveness. This makes the capital-intensity of the model structural rather than cyclical, since equipment refresh competes for the same capital as network expansion.
- Cybersecurity and patient-data privacy exposure — Increasing reliance on digital platforms, laboratory information systems and cloud-based applications exposes the Company to cyber threats, data breaches and unauthorised access to patient information. Any such incident may disrupt operations and damage reputation and stakeholder trust - a heightened concern as the AR also flags evolving data protection requirements as a regulatory risk.
- Equipment downtime and third-party supply-chain dependency — Pathology and radiology operations rely extensively on sophisticated diagnostic equipment, and prolonged malfunction, breakdown or delay in maintenance or replacement may disrupt service delivery. The Company also depends on third-party suppliers for reagents, consumables, radiology equipment and specialised diagnostic materials, so any supply disruption can affect testing capability and operational continuity; mitigation is preventive maintenance protocols, multiple supplier relationships, inventory management and vendor diversification.

business.body: Suraksha Diagnostic Limited, founded in 1992 by Dr. Somnath Chatterjee along with Late Kishan Kumar Kejriwal, operates an integrated network of laboratories, diagnostic centres and sample collection centres delivering pathology, radiology and specialised healthcare services. outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: FY26 was a year of network build-out. The Company expanded across high-density, underserved markets in West Bengal and neighbouring regions by adding two hub centres, 11 spoke centres and three PPP centres, taking the total network to 68 centres as at 31 March 2026. Management states these investments, together with the ramp-up of the new centres, had a near-term impact on margins - EBITDA margin was 31.8% against 33.8% in the prior year - while strengthening the foundation for later years. Capability expansion ran alongside footprint expansion: the Company launched Suraksha Genomics, its specialised genomics and molecular diagnostics vertical, and acquired a 63% stake in Fetomat Wellness Private Limited, a foetal and maternal medicine network in Eastern India. A notable equipment milestone was the deployment of next-generation 1.5T helium-free MRI technology at Calcutta Medical College, which management says enhances diagnostic capability across neurology, orthopaedics, cardiology and oncology, supports faster patient throughput and reduces resource consumption and maintenance requirements. The Company also collaborated with IIT Kharagpur on two research projects, one developing an AI-driven solution for early detection of Alzheimer's disease from routine brain MRI scans with clinical trials already underway, and expanded specialised clinical offerings with dedicated dementia, epilepsy and gynaecology-led clinics plus initiatives for early detection of cervical and ovarian cancers. Looking forward, the stated FY27 plan is to establish three hub centres and eight asset-light spoke centres across West Bengal, leveraging the existing central reference laboratory infrastructure, and to set up specialised hub centres in Bihar, Tripura and Jharkhand beyond the core market. The MD&A opportunity discussion frames a planned expansion to 100 centres by FY28 alongside entry into underserved Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities beyond Eastern India, expected to improve operational leverage. Management describes the approach as calibrated and data-driven, supported by detailed market assessments and phased implementation under the hub-and-spoke operating model, and flags execution risk - delays in operationalisation, lower-than-expected utilisation, longer gestation and variability in new-centre performance - as well as constraints in sourcing trained technicians and specialised personnel in new geographies. The AR states no rupee capital-expenditure quantum in the narrative, and the capital-commitments named disclosure supplied carries only the caption with no readable figure or unit.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- India's diagnostics industry is projected to grow at a CAGR of approximately 12% over the next five years to a market size of around Rs 1.25-1.30 lakh crore, driven primarily by volume expansion rather than price
- The Indian market remains highly fragmented with over 1.3 lakh laboratories; organised players account for only approximately 20-25% of the market, leaving significant scope for consolidation and formalisation that favours integrated chains
- Standalone laboratories still held a 42% market share in FY 2025-26; large-format organised chains are gaining share from standalone laboratories as patients prefer quality assurance, faster turnaround and wider service capability
- Pathology remains the largest segment at 65% of the Indian market in FY 2025-26; urban areas dominate with a 70% share reflecting advanced infrastructure, insurance penetration and disposable income
- Pricing is expected to remain stable with realisations growing only modestly at around 1-2% annually, making growth volume-led and operating efficiency the profit lever
- Preventive and wellness testing is a sustained growth driver, supported by rising health awareness, lifestyle-related disorders and emphasis on early detection across urban and semi-urban markets
- Expansion into Tier 2, 3 and 4 cities, supported by improving infrastructure and rising insurance penetration, is expected to widen market access and unlock new demand pools
- Adoption of molecular diagnostics, genomics and next-generation sequencing is transforming disease detection and treatment pathways, supporting the shift into higher-value precision diagnostics
- Digital transformation - LIMS, AI-enabled tools, cloud platforms, home sample collection and point-of-care testing - is reshaping service delivery, improving turnaround and reducing errors
- Government support: healthcare allocation in the Union Budget 2026-27 increased to approximately Rs 1.06 lakh crore, and initiatives including Ayushman Bharat and the PLI scheme are improving access and domestic equipment manufacturing
- Over the past five years, industry patient volumes and test sample volumes grew at a CAGR of approximately 12% and 17% respectively, while realisation per test moderated on competitive intensity and improved affordability
- Globally, the clinical diagnostics market is projected at USD 213.03 billion in FY 2025-26 and expected to grow from USD 203.24 billion in 2024 to USD 264.12 billion in FY 2032-33
- Macro backdrop: India's real GDP growth estimated at 7.7% in FY 2025-26 and projected at 6.6% for FY 2026-27, with inflation projected at 5.1%; RBI cut policy rates by a cumulative 125 basis points since February 2025
- Headwind - supply chain complexity and cost volatility, as diagnostics relies heavily on globally sourced equipment and consumables exposed to disruptions, tariffs and trade uncertainty
- Headwind - pricing pressure and competitive intensity from organised chains, hospital-based laboratories and low-cost providers keeping realisation per test under stress
- Headwind - evolving regulatory and compliance requirements, with variations in standards, licensing and quality controls across regions increasing operational complexity
- Headwind - advanced technology adoption requires significant upfront investment in infrastructure and digital systems, a barrier that widens the gap between organised and unorganised players

risks.risk: Execution risk in the network expansion strategy

risks.note: The Company describes itself as one of the largest full-service integrated diagnostic chains in Eastern India, headquartered in Kolkata, with its operating network across West Bengal, Bihar, Assam and Meghalaya. risks.risk: Geographic concentration in Eastern and North-Eastern India

risks.note: The business is heavily dependent on experienced radiologists, pathologists, technicians and healthcare professionals; shortage of qualified personnel, rising attrition or an inability to attract and retain talent may impair service quality and operational efficiency. risks.risk: Dependence on scarce skilled medical professionals and attrition

risks.note: The Company operates in a highly regulated environment subject to healthcare and diagnostic laws, regulations and quality standards. risks.risk: Regulatory, pricing-control and data-protection compliance burden

risks.note: Rapid advances in diagnostic technology require continuous investment in equipment upgrades and technology integration; failure to adopt evolving technologies may erode service quality and competitiveness. This makes the capital-intensity of the model structural rather than cyclical, since equipment refresh competes for the same capital as network expansion.
risks.risk: Technological obsolescence in radiology, pathology and molecular diagnostics

risks.note: Increasing reliance on digital platforms, laboratory information systems and cloud-based applications exposes the Company to cyber threats, data breaches and unauthorised access to patient information. Any such incident may disrupt operations and damage reputation and stakeholder trust - a heightened concern as the AR also flags evolving data protection requirements as a regulatory risk.

Pathology and radiology operations rely extensively on sophisticated diagnostic equipment, and prolonged malfunction, breakdown or delay in maintenance or replacement may disrupt service delivery. The Company also depends on third-party suppliers for reagents, consumables, radiology equipment and specialised diagnostic materials, so any supply disruption can affect testing capability and operational continuity; mitigation is preventive maintenance protocols, multiple supplier relationships, inventory management and vendor diversification.

risks.risk: Intensifying competition and consequent pricing pressure
risks.note: The AR flags a highly competitive diagnostics industry where national diagnostic chains, hospital-based laboratories, regional standalone players and digital-first healthcare platforms are expanding aggressively, which may cause pricing pressure, loss of market share and margin contraction in the Company's key operating regions. Management separately lists pricing risk from competition, customer expectations and potential regulatory intervention, and notes that unorganised, low-cost participants create pricing pressure and can dilute brand perception on quality and pricing standards.

risks.risk: Execution risk in the network expansion strategy
risks.note: Growth depends on adding new centres and laboratories, which exposes the Company to delays in operationalisation, lower-than-expected utilisation, longer gestation periods and variability in the performance of new centres - all of which can weigh on short-term profitability. This is the direct counterweight to the stated plan of expanding to 100 centres by FY28 and entering Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities beyond Eastern India.

risks.risk: Geographic concentration in Eastern and North-Eastern India
risks.note: The Company describes itself as one of the largest full-service integrated diagnostic chains in Eastern India, headquartered in Kolkata, with its operating network across West Bengal, Bihar, Assam and Meghalaya. Earnings are therefore tied to demand, competition and regulation in a single contiguous region, and the diversification remedy the AR points to - Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities beyond Eastern India - is still a plan rather than an established base.

risks.risk: Dependence on scarce skilled medical professionals and attrition
risks.note: The business is heavily dependent on experienced radiologists, pathologists, technicians and healthcare professionals; shortage of qualified personnel, rising attrition or an inability to attract and retain talent may impair service quality and operational efficiency. Management also flags that limited availability of adequately trained technicians and specialised personnel in new geographies may itself slow the pace of expansion, forcing redeployment of experienced staff from existing centres.

risks.risk: Regulatory, pricing-control and data-protection compliance burden
risks.note: The Company operates in a highly regulated environment subject to healthcare and diagnostic laws, regulations and quality standards. Changes in government regulations, pricing controls, data protection requirements or healthcare policies may raise compliance costs and reduce operational flexibility; mitigation rests on internal compliance mechanisms, compliance audits and monitoring of regulatory developments.

risks.risk: Technological obsolescence in radiology, pathology and molecular diagnostics
risks.note: Rapid advances in diagnostic technology require continuous investment in equipment upgrades and technology integration; failure to adopt evolving technologies may erode service quality and competitiveness. This makes the capital-intensity of the model structural rather than cyclical, since equipment refresh competes for the same capital as network expansion.

Increasing reliance on digital platforms, laboratory information systems and cloud-based applications exposes the Company to cyber threats, data breaches and unauthorised access to patient information. Any such incident may disrupt operations and damage reputation and stakeholder trust - a heightened concern as the AR also flags evolving data protection requirements as a regulatory risk.

risks.risk: Equipment downtime and third-party supply-chain dependency
risks.note: Pathology and radiology operations rely extensively on sophisticated diagnostic equipment, and prolonged malfunction, breakdown or delay in maintenance or replacement may disrupt service delivery. The Company also depends on third-party suppliers for reagents, consumables, radiology equipment and specialised diagnostic materials, so any supply disruption can affect testing capability and operational continuity; mitigation is preventive maintenance protocols, multiple supplier relationships, inventory management and vendor diversification.

one_liner.body: An integrated diagnostics provider offering pathology, radiology and medical consultation under one roof through a hub-and-spoke network of 68 diagnostic centres across Eastern and North-Eastern India.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Suraksha Diagnostic Limited, founded in 1992 by Dr. Somnath Chatterjee along with Late Kishan Kumar Kejriwal, operates an integrated network of laboratories, diagnostic centres and sample collection centres delivering pathology, radiology and specialised healthcare services. Its one-stop model spans routine and specialised pathology, basic to advanced radiology, preventive health packages, doctor consultations, polyclinic services and home collection, serving patients directly (B2C) as well as hospitals, corporates and institutional clients (B2B). Operations run on a hub-and-spoke architecture in which a central reference laboratory and satellite labs process samples routed from hub and spoke centres and collection points.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India's diagnostics industry is projected to grow at a CAGR of approximately 12% over the next five years to a market size of around Rs 1.25-1.30 lakh crore, driven primarily by volume expansion rather than price
- The Indian market remains highly fragmented with over 1.3 lakh laboratories; organised players account for only approximately 20-25% of the market, leaving significant scope for consolidation and formalisation that favours integrated chains
- Standalone laboratories still held a 42% market share in FY 2025-26; large-format organised chains are gaining share from standalone laboratories as patients prefer quality assurance, faster turnaround and wider service capability
- Pathology remains the largest segment at 65% of the Indian market in FY 2025-26; urban areas dominate with a 70% share reflecting advanced infrastructure, insurance penetration and disposable income
- Pricing is expected to remain stable with realisations growing only modestly at around 1-2% annually, making growth volume-led and operating efficiency the profit lever
- Preventive and wellness testing is a sustained growth driver, supported by rising health awareness, lifestyle-related disorders and emphasis on early detection across urban and semi-urban markets
- Expansion into Tier 2, 3 and 4 cities, supported by improving infrastructure and rising insurance penetration, is expected to widen market access and unlock new demand pools
- Adoption of molecular diagnostics, genomics and next-generation sequencing is transforming disease detection and treatment pathways, supporting the shift into higher-value precision diagnostics
- Digital transformation - LIMS, AI-enabled tools, cloud platforms, home sample collection and point-of-care testing - is reshaping service delivery, improving turnaround and reducing errors
- Government support: healthcare allocation in the Union Budget 2026-27 increased to approximately Rs 1.06 lakh crore, and initiatives including Ayushman Bharat and the PLI scheme are improving access and domestic equipment manufacturing
- Over the past five years, industry patient volumes and test sample volumes grew at a CAGR of approximately 12% and 17% respectively, while realisation per test moderated on competitive intensity and improved affordability
- Globally, the clinical diagnostics market is projected at USD 213.03 billion in FY 2025-26 and expected to grow from USD 203.24 billion in 2024 to USD 264.12 billion in FY 2032-33
- Macro backdrop: India's real GDP growth estimated at 7.7% in FY 2025-26 and projected at 6.6% for FY 2026-27, with inflation projected at 5.1%; RBI cut policy rates by a cumulative 125 basis points since February 2025

- Headwind - evolving regulatory and compliance requirements, with variations in standards, licensing and quality controls across regions increasing operational complexity

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: FY26 was a year of network build-out. The Company expanded across high-density, underserved markets in West Bengal and neighbouring regions by adding two hub centres, 11 spoke centres and three PPP centres, taking the total network to 68 centres as at 31 March 2026. Management states these investments, together with the ramp-up of the new centres, had a near-term impact on margins - EBITDA margin was 31.8% against 33.8% in the prior year - while strengthening the foundation for later years. Capability expansion ran alongside footprint expansion: the Company launched Suraksha Genomics, its specialised genomics and molecular diagnostics vertical, and acquired a 63% stake in Fetomat Wellness Private Limited, a foetal and maternal medicine network in Eastern India. A notable equipment milestone was the deployment of next-generation 1.5T helium-free MRI technology at Calcutta Medical College, which management says enhances diagnostic capability across neurology, orthopaedics, cardiology and oncology, supports faster patient throughput and reduces resource consumption and maintenance requirements. Looking forward, the stated FY27 plan is to establish three hub centres and eight asset-light spoke centres across West Bengal, leveraging the existing central reference laboratory infrastructure, and to set up specialised hub centres in Bihar, Tripura and Jharkhand beyond the core market. The MD&A opportunity discussion frames a planned expansion to 100 centres by FY28 alongside entry into underserved Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities beyond Eastern India, expected to improve operational leverage. Management describes the approach as calibrated and data-driven, supported by detailed market assessments and phased implementation under the hub-and-spoke operating model, and flags execution risk - delays in operationalisation, lower-than-expected utilisation, longer gestation and variability in new-centre performance - as well as constraints in sourcing trained technicians and specialised personnel in new geographies. segment / subsidiary detail: Pathology (48.85% rev, high consumable cost); Radiology (44.26% rev, lower consumable/higher reporting cost, 1.5T helium-free MRI deployed); Consultancy (6.89% rev, 85% fee payout to doctors); Genomics (INR 1 Cr in Q4, INR 3.5 Mn/month run-rate, fast-turnaround NGS platform).
growth verticals / optionality: Geographic expansion into Bihar, Jharkhand, Tripura, and Assam (Guwahati traction); Genomics scaling (oncology/prenatal); AI integration (Alzheimer's detection pilot with IIT Kharagpur); Specialty clinics (Dementia, Epilepsy, Gyne-oncology).
margins & cost dynamics: Blended EBITDA margin 31.8% (-200bps YoY) due to new center pre-operating expenses and fixed cost absorption. Mature centers deliver 36-37% margins. New centers (<2 yrs) at -5.5% EBITDA. Breakeven: 5-6 months (small), 9-12 months (large) at center level; +1-2 quarters for HO expense absorption. Professional fees (doctors) ~16-17% of revenue (variable cost). Rental cost ~INR 30 Cr/year.
capex / expansion: FY27 planned capex ~INR 70 Cr for 5 hubs and 8 spokes. Recent investments include Genexus NGS platform, 1.5T helium-free MRI at Calcutta Medical College, Roche automation in pathology labs.

management quality / tone: Confident on long-term structural growth and technology leadership; Conservative on short-term guidance (15% rev growth) to account for expansion drag; Transparent about margin compression being temporary due to ramp-up; Defensive on patient growth metrics citing data hygiene flaws.

themes.need: Under-bedded India plus insurance penetration and preventive-care adoption drive a domestic healthcare capex + volume cycle distinct from export pharma.
